Your product development is like an airport. Agents are taking off from the terminal, spin their engines and generate trails before they land again. To prevent any unnecessary delays, a short turnaround time is crucial.

The check-in process in Agent Airport International (AAI) is operated by Entire, so the high throughput is handled smoothly.

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled — the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Each question should be formatted like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree — settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it — don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report — ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's — put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

Links: [{"title":"Herdr – terminal-based agent multiplexer","url":"https://www.linuxlinks.com/herdr-terminal-based-agent-multiplexer/"},{"title":"Herdr alternatives for running coding agents","url":"https://flaviocopes.com/herdr-alternatives/"},{"title":"A deep dive into Herdr","url":"https://flaviocopes.com/herdr/"},{"title":"# A deep dive into Herdr","url":"https://flaviocopes.com/herdr.md"},{"title":"herdr: A Terminal Tool for Managing Multiple AI Coding Agents","url":"https://tecmint.com/herdr-run-ai-coding-agents-in-linux-terminal"},{"title":"docsearch.algolia.com","url":"https://docsearch.algolia.com/mcp/docs/repo/ogulcancelik/herdr"},{"title":"herdr  by ogulcancelik","url":"https://www.sourcepulse.org/projects/28273906"},{"title":"Agent multiplexer · a binary, not an app","url":"https://herdr.dev/token/"},{"title":"Agent multiplexer · a binary, not an app","url":"https://herdr.dev/docs/remote"},{"title":"herdr: manage multiple AI coding agents in one terminal","url":"https://knightli.com/en/2026/07/06/herdr-terminal-agent-multiplexer/"}]

Herdr is a terminal-based multiplexer built for running coding agents, positioned as a tmux-style alternative that understands what each agent is doing.

- **Core idea:** Herdr is a tmux redesigned for agents: each agent runs in a real terminal, while herdr organizes them into workspaces, tabs, and panes, and it shows whether each agent is blocked, working, done, or idle.
- **Why it differs from tmux:** tmux sees each pane as just a command, so it can't tell you which of your ten agents is waiting for approval.
- **Persistence:** Like tmux, pane processes keep running in the background after you detach, and you can reattach later. It also runs on any machine you can ssh into, and you can attach from a phone.
- **Control and scripting:** Herdr provides a background server, state awareness, and a Socket API for agent-to-agent interaction. Its CLI and socket API let a script or an agent create workspaces, start agents, and read results.
- **Supported agents:** Per one source, it works with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Devin, Cursor Agent, or other CLI agents.
- **Project details:** It is written in Rust and licensed under the AGPL v3. One source says it has been one of the top trending projects on GitHub since late June 2026, and another gives the latest release as v0.7.1.

**Alternatives:** Flavio Copes suggests tmux if you want the most portable option, with workmux added for worktrees and agent status. He recommends cmux on a Mac and worktrunk as a worktree manager to use alongside Herdr.

Sources conflict slightly on details. For example, one site describes the project as a "terminal-native supervisor" while another calls it a "workspace manager." The main sources are herdr.dev, the GitHub repo at github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr, and the reviews by Flavio Copes and TecMint.

input.prompt:
I am preparing a hackathon pitch (Agentic AI Hack Zürich, 10 Oct 2026, hosted by Entire with Google DeepMind). Our product idea: a visual "air traffic control" dashboard over many parallel coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) running inside Herdr. Gemini ranks which waiting agent the developer should handle next. Find facts only, from primary sources (official sites, docs, GitHub READMEs). Report concisely.

1. Entire (entire.io, hack.entire.io/agentic-ai-hack-zurich-2026/): What is the product? What do "Trails", "checkpoints", "Continuous Memory" (entire-graph, entire-brain), and the `entire` CLI do? What data does it capture about agent sessions, and can a third-party tool read it (API, MCP, files in repo)? List the ten suggested project ideas on the hackathon page verbatim if possible. Find any judging criteria, prizes, sponsor tracks, pitch length or demo format for this hackathon.
2. Herdr (herdr.dev, github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr): What does the socket API / CLI expose? Specifically: can an external program (a) list all agents/panes with their state (blocked, working, done, idle), (b) read a pane's recent terminal output, (c) send keystrokes or text input to a pane, (d) subscribe to state change events? Give the relevant command or API names.

Mark anything you could not confirm as unconfirmed.

content.text:
I read the brief and the event page. Three facts shape the questions below.

1. The brief judges projects on four tests. The agent must act, it must help a named person, people must stay in control, and it must work live at 8pm with real inputs.
2. Herdr already shows whether each agent is blocked, working, done or idle. It also has a socket API that scripts can use. So "Herdr has no status indication" is not a strong claim, but "Herdr has no prioritization" still holds.
3. The event page does not list judging criteria, prizes or the pitch length.

A sub-agent is now checking what Entire's tools and Herdr's socket API can do. Questions that depend on those facts wait for the next round.

❓ **Q1** - **One metaphor or two**: The draft uses two metaphors. The solution section describes a city with houses and streets. The pitch describes an airport with planes, a control tower and ground control. The name "Plane Sight" only works with the airport. Two metaphors in one pitch confuse the audience.

➡️ Use the airport everywhere, including the UI. Show a pixel-art airport from above. Gates group related agents, which keeps your 2D grouping idea. The runway queue shows priority order. Planes in the air are agents that are working, so they are hidden or faded.

❓ **Q2** - **The one problem you lead with**: The draft lists six problems: cognitive overload, prioritization, 1D lists, context switching, dependencies and understanding what agents did. A short pitch can carry one problem well and perhaps mention a second.

➡️ Lead with prioritization ("which agent do I handle next?"). Your closing line already says this. Use cognitive overload as the emotional setup. Mention the other four as roadmap items, or leave them out.

❓ **Q3** - **What the agent does beyond ranking**: The brief's first test says the agent must act, not only answer. A ranking alone is close to "only answering". Here are three options:
- (a) Gemini ranks the waiting agents, and nothing more.
- (b) Gemini ranks them and also drafts the reply for each one, such as "approve this tool call" or "pick option B, because…". You confirm with one key, and Herdr sends the reply to the agent.
- (c) Gemini handles low-risk prompts by itself, such as read-only tool approvals, and sends only the rest to you.

➡️ Choose (b), and add (c) only for clearly safe cases if time permits. Option (b) passes the "acts" test and the "people stay in control" test together, and it matches the brief's "human checkpoint" pattern. This assumes Herdr can send input to a pane. The sub-agent is checking that now.

❓ **Q4** - **What color means**: The draft uses color for two different things. The "Setting" section uses color for the type of input the agent needs, such as tool approval, design decision or QA. The "Solution" section uses color for the task type, such as bugfix, planning or implementing. The task-type list also uses green twice.

➡️ Use color for the type of input the agent needs from you. That is the information you need in order to prioritize. Show the task type as a label or an icon on the plane. Keep "pulse = working, bright = needs you".

❓ **Q5** - **Personalization and "Jev"**: The draft says that each decision you make trains a decision agent called Jev. A learning system is hard to show in a one-day live demo. I also do not know what Jev is. Is it a teammate's project, a product, or a name you invented?

➡️ Keep a simple version. Store your past choices and give the last N of them to Gemini as context, then pitch it as "it learns your priorities". Drop the name Jev unless it refers to something real, because a third name for an agent dilutes "Gemini is the controller".

❓ **Q6** - **Dependencies between agents**: The pitch says that Plane Sight finds dependencies "so they don't collide". To build that, you must detect dependencies, for example agents that edit the same files or the same branch.

➡️ Build only the simple case. Flag two agents as a possible collision when they touch the same files, which you can read from git. Do not draw streets or dependency lines. If time runs out, cut this feature and remove the claim from the pitch.

❓ **Q7** - **Pitch length and format**: The event page does not give the pitch length or the demo format. Do you know them? For example, 3 minutes with a live demo, or 2 minutes of slides plus 2 minutes of demo.

➡️ If you do not know, plan for 3 minutes in total with a live demo, and ask the organizers today.

❓ **Q8** - **How the live demo stays reliable**: The brief requires real inputs at 8pm. Real agents are slow and unpredictable, so your demo moment may not happen on cue.

➡️ Before you go on stage, start about 8 real agents in Herdr on a prepared repo. Give them tasks that stop at known points, such as a permission prompt, a design question or a failing test. That way the "back from lunch" screen is real and is already waiting when you open it.

Sources:
- [Agentic AI Hack Zürich event page](https://hack.entire.io/agentic-ai-hack-zurich-2026/)
- [A deep dive into Herdr (Flavio Copes)](https://flaviocopes.com/herdr/)
- [herdr: A Terminal Tool for Managing Multiple AI Coding Agents (TecMint)](https://tecmint.com/herdr-run-ai-coding-agents-in-linux-terminal)
- [herdr.dev](https://herdr.dev/docs/remote)

Q2 agreed

Q4 sounds good

Q7 yes 
Q8 yes

I am taking your Q7 answer to mean that you do not know the format yet. So we plan for 3 minutes in total with a live demo, and you confirm the format with the organizers. The sub-agent is still checking Entire and Herdr. The questions about Entire's role wait for its report.

❓ **Q9** - **The opening hook**: The draft lists four openings: the overloaded developer, usage statistics, "coding is not fun anymore", and the city mayor. The mayor no longer fits, because you chose the airport. Statistics only work if you have a real source, and an invented curve hurts your credibility with technical judges.

➡️ Open with the "back from lunch" scene, and show it on screen. Display 8 real Herdr panes that are all waiting, and say one line, for example "Which one first?". Then switch to Plane Sight. Drop the statistics unless you have a source, and say "we run 8 agents ourselves" instead.

❓ **Q10** - **How you position Herdr**: The draft calls Herdr the current solution and lists its weaknesses. Later, it uses Herdr as your backend. Herdr already shows which agents are blocked. If you criticize the tool you build on, the audience will be confused, and a Herdr person may be in the room.

➡️ Present Herdr as the base layer: "Herdr tells you which agents are blocked. Plane Sight tells you which one to handle first and what to answer." Keep "ground control" as Herdr's role in the metaphor.

❓ **Q11** - **How Gemini ranks**: "Most urgent" needs a rule that you can explain in one sentence on stage. Here are some candidate signals:
- How long the agent has waited.
- How fast you can answer. A quick approval is faster than a design decision.
- How much other work it unblocks.
- How important the task is.
- Your learned preferences (Q5).

➡️ Use "the most unblocked work per second of your attention". Quick approvals come first, then decisions that unblock other agents, then reviews. Your past choices change the order. On stage, show one line of reasoning for each plane, so the ranking does not look arbitrary.

❓ **Q12** - **What a gate means**: You chose gates as the 2D grouping. Each gate needs one clear grouping rule. Here are three options:
- (a) One gate per repository or worktree.
- (b) Gemini groups agents by feature, for example "the 3 UI agents".
- (c) You assign gates by hand.

➡️ Choose (a). It is reliable and fast to build, and it matches how collisions happen, because agents in the same repository can collide. Option (b) looks smarter, but it can group agents wrongly during the live demo.

❓ **Q13** - **Pitch structure for 3 minutes**: The draft spends most of its words on the airport analogy, which you tell before you show anything. The judges score the live demo, so the demo needs most of the time.

➡️ Use this outline:
- 0:00–0:20: The hook (Q9).
- 0:20–0:40: The problem. You run many agents, the 1D list gives no priority, and you switch context constantly.
- 0:40–2:20: The live demo. The airport opens and in-flight planes are faded. Gemini puts the waiting planes in a queue. You open the first plane and see a summary and a drafted reply. You approve it with one key, and the plane takes off. You also show one collision warning.
- 2:20–2:45: The architecture in airport words. Gemini is the control tower, Herdr is ground control, and Entire's role depends on Q14 in the next round.
- 2:45–3:00: The closing line, which you already have.

Tell the airport story during the demo, and do not tell it as a separate section first.

  Research report: Entire and Herdr facts for the Agentic AI Hack Zürich pitch. All facts come from primary sources: the hackathon page, docs.entire.io, the herdrdev/herdr repo docs, and the brief PDF in the repo. Unconfirmed items are marked.
  
  ## 1. Entire
  
  **What it is.** The hackathon page says: "Entire is the git forge for AI-native teams. The Entire CLI captures every AI coding agent session, so the reasoning behind the code stays with the git repo, right next to your code." Continuous Memory turns those sessions into knowledge that agents can use. It also offers Git hosting and mirrors of GitHub repos.
  
  **Concepts**
  - **Checkpoint:** a save point that links a Git commit to the agent sessions and decisions behind it. The link is made with the commit trailers `Entire-Checkpoint` and `Entire-Attribution`. `Entire-Attribution` records how many lines came from the agent and how many from a human.
  - **Trail:** from the glossary: "Entire's unit of work, covering one branch and one pull request from one intent to shipped code." A Trail groups the intent, the checkpoints, and a rolled-up summary and report. Teams review the Trail instead of the raw diff.
    - Each Trail is backed by a GitHub PR for CI.
    - Runners are AI agents that run in cloud sandboxes and are defined in `.entire/runners/`. They evaluate each push and raise findings, with scores for risk, drift, confidence and security. Open findings block the merge.
    - Trails is behind a feature flag. You request access with a form.
    - Commands: `entire runner setup -y` and `entire trail create`.
  - **Continuous Memory** is Graph plus Brain.
    - **entire-graph** is a plugin that gives agents a map of the codebase: implementations, relationships and change impact. Entire claims it saves up to 71% of token spend. Commands: `entire plugin install graph`, `entire graph init-agents --repo .` and `entire graph stats --repo .`. The stats command reads Claude Code transcripts to estimate the tokens saved.
    - **entire-brain** is a memory layer that lives in the repo: sessions, checkpoints, facts, docs and code structure. It carries context across agents, for example from Claude Code to Codex. Commands: `entire brain setup`, `entire brain status` and `entire brain init-agents`. A background watcher extracts facts from sessions, and that extraction uses an agent and costs tokens.
  
  **Other CLI commands:** `entire enable`, `entire status`, `entire session list|current|info|tokens|stop|attach|adopt|resume`, `entire checkpoint list|explain`, `entire search` (semantic, or `--code` for literal text), `entire why`, `entire blame`, `entire recap`, `entire dispatch`, `entire review`, `entire investigate`, `entire tokens`, `entire doctor` and `entire api`.
  
  **What it captures.** For Claude Code, hooks in `.claude/settings.json` capture session boundaries, prompts, completed turns and task events. Entire then reads the full conversation, file changes, tool calls and token usage from the JSONL transcripts, including subagent sessions. A session holds prompts, responses, code changes, checkpoints, token usage, metadata and line attribution. `session info` shows the agent, model, status, worktree, timing, tokens, checkpoint links and files touched. Built-in integrations are Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot CLI, Antigravity, Factory, OpenCode and Pi. Other agents can be added through the Agent Integration Protocol.
  
  **Can a third-party tool read it? Yes, in several ways.**
  - **Files in the repo, readable with plain Git:**
    - The default backend stores one ref per checkpoint at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<ULID>`. List them with `git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints/`.
    - Repos enabled before CLI 0.10.0 use the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch instead.
    - During an active session, checkpoints sit on local shadow branches named `entire/<commit>-<worktree>`, which are never pushed.
    - Settings live in `.entire/settings.json`.
  - **CLI JSON:** `entire session list --json`, `entire session info ID --json`, `entire session current --json` and `entire status --json` all return JSON. `--transcript` streams the raw transcript.
  - **MCP:**
    - `entire mcp` is a read-only stdio server with only two tools: `agent_help` and `entire_status`.
    - `entire brain mcp` is Brain's MCP server. I did not check its tools list.
    - The docs themselves are an MCP server at `https://docs.entire.io/mcp`.
  - **HTTP API:** `entire api PATH` makes authenticated requests. OpenAPI specs are listed in docs.entire.io/llms.txt, but the docs warn these are "internal endpoints [that] may change without notice."
  
  **For our idea:** Entire's session states are active, stale and stopped (plus resumed, adopted, attached and imported). It does not report whether an agent is blocked or waiting for input. Herdr is the source for that.
  
  **The ten suggested ideas (verbatim titles and descriptions)**
  1. **Hand off work between agents without losing context.** "Start a feature in Claude Code and finish it in Codex. Use Brain to carry the decisions and rejected approaches across, and Graph to point both agents at the same code. Show the second agent picking up the work without being re-briefed."
  2. **Prove what Continuous Memory saves.** "Run the same set of tasks with and without Graph and Brain. Compare tokens, time and correctness, using entire graph stats for the token savings, and publish the results with links to the sessions behind each run."
  3. **A debugger for agent mistakes.** "Start with a failing test or bug, inspect the affected code with Graph, and trace relevant checkpoints to find where an incorrect assumption entered the implementation. Show the evidence behind the diagnosis."
  4. **A reviewer that checks intent.** "Compare the original request with the committed change. Flag missed requirements, unexpected behavior, and claims that lack test evidence, with links to the relevant transcript and code."
  5. **A "before you build" assistant.** "Search previous sessions for similar attempts and rejected approaches, then use Graph to locate reusable code. Produce a short briefing before the agent starts editing."
  6. **An architecture drift detector.** "Compare Graph snapshots across commits to spot new dependencies or unexpected coupling. Attach checkpoint context explaining why each change was introduced."
  7. **An onboarding guide you can question.** "Let a new teammate ask, "How does authentication work, and why was it designed this way?" Combine current code relationships with historical decisions and source links."
  8. **A regression test scout.** "Use a checkpoint's changes and Graph relationships to suggest behaviors that need tests. Consult session context for edge cases the agent discussed but may not have covered."
  9. **A checkpoint-to-demo generator.** "Turn a checkpoint into a concise walkthrough: the problem, key decisions, implementation, and recorded validation. Generate a shareable page with links back to the evidence."
  10. **An integration for your favorite unsupported agent.** "Build an adapter that captures its sessions and connects them to commits. Ship it with lifecycle tests and a working checkpoint demo."
  - **Other:** "Feel free to be creative and impress!"
  
  **Event logistics**
  - The event runs 10 Oct 2026, 09:30–21:30 CEST. Joseph Katsioloudes (Developer Relations) is on site for Entire.
  - The brief PDF in the repo calls it the "Open innovation track", supported by Google DeepMind, and says "we want every team to build with Gemini".
  - The brief lists four tests that strong projects pass. These are not labelled as judging criteria:
    - it acts: it plans, uses tools and finishes tasks
    - it helps someone real
    - people stay in control: it asks before doing anything irreversible
    - it works live: "you can demo it at 8pm with real inputs"
  - The recommended model for planning, reasoning and code is `gemini-3.8-flash`, called through the Interactions API.
  - **Unconfirmed:** formal judging criteria, prizes, a separate Entire sponsor track, pitch length and demo format. None of these appear on the Entire page or in the brief, and web searches found no event page with them.
  
  ## 2. Herdr
  
  The repo `ogulcancelik/herdr` now redirects to `herdrdev/herdr`. Herdr marks every pane as working, blocked or idle. It talks over newline-delimited JSON on a Unix socket at `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`, which can be overridden with `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH` or `HERDR_SESSION`. `herdr api schema` prints the JSON Schema. The methods below appear in both the released 0.9.3 docs and the next-version docs.
  
  | Need | Supported? | CLI | Socket method |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | (a) List agents and panes with their state | Yes | `herdr agent list`, `herdr agent get <target>`, `herdr pane list`, `herdr api snapshot` | `agent.list`, `agent.get`, `pane.list`, `pane.get`, `session.snapshot` |
  | (b) Read a pane's recent output | Yes | `herdr pane read <id> --source visible\|recent\|recent-unwrapped\|detection --lines N [--ansi]`, `herdr agent read <target> ...` | `pane.read`, `agent.read` |
  | (c) Send keys or text to a pane | Yes | `herdr pane send-text <id> <text>`, `herdr pane send-keys <id> enter ...`, `herdr pane run <id> <cmd>`, `herdr agent send-keys`, `herdr agent prompt <target> <text> [--wait --until STATUS]` | `pane.send_text`, `pane.send_keys`, `pane.send_input`, `agent.send_keys`, `agent.prompt` |
  | (d) Subscribe to state-change events | Yes | `herdr agent wait <target> --until blocked\|done` (one-shot) | `events.subscribe`, `events.wait` |
  
  Details:
  - **(a) States:** the status values are `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, `done` and `unknown`.
    - `done` means idle but not yet seen. Focusing the pane marks it seen.
    - `blocked` means Herdr recognised an approval or question UI.
    - `pane_info` includes `agent_status`. `agent.explain` shows why Herdr classified a pane the way it did.
  - **(c) Prompt caveat:** `agent.prompt` refuses to send input to a `blocked` agent and returns `agent_blocked`. To answer an approval prompt, use `send-keys` or `send-text` instead.
  - **(d) Events:**
    - Example subscription: `{"method":"events.subscribe","params":{"subscriptions":[{"type":"pane.agent_status_changed","pane_id":"w1:p1","agent_status":"blocked"}]}}`

# herdr smoke test: herdr panes plus our own hooks server (option F)

This is step 1 of the build plan in `research/game-server-backend.md` section 5.2. herdr creates the worktree and starts each agent. Our hooks server (a copy of `../hooks/server.mjs` that also logs `X-Herdr-Pane`) receives the hook events and holds approvals and questions.

Tested on 2026-10-10 with herdr client 0.9.3 (server 0.9.1), Claude Code 2.1.296 (Haiku) and Codex CLI 0.161.0.

## Results

| # | Check | Claude Code | Codex |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `herdr worktree create` + `herdr agent start` with our hook flags | Works. Stops once at the folder trust prompt (`agent_not_ready`). `agent send-keys u1 down enter` answers it. | Works. Stops at an update prompt and then a folder trust prompt. herdr reported `idle` during the update prompt, which was wrong. |
| 2 | Hook POST carries `X-Herdr-Pane` | Yes, `w1B:p1`, through `headers` + `allowedEnvVars` | Yes, `w1C:p1`, from `$HERDR_PANE_ID` in `codex-hook.sh` |
| 3 | Hook `session_id` equals herdr `agent_session.value` | Yes (`ee39ffe3…`) | Yes (`01a125dc…`) |
| 4 | Deny with a reason changes what the agent does | Yes, with the right wording (see below) | Yes. It stopped and said it would wait. |
| 5 | `herdr agent prompt` while the agent is busy | Yes. The order was queued and followed. | Yes. The order was queued and followed. |
| 6 | herdr status while our server holds a request | Approval: `blocked`. Question: `working`. | Approval: `working` (Codex shows only "Running hook"). |
| 7 | Claude question answered from the server | Yes. "User answered Claude's questions: → Blue" | Not tested |

## Findings that matter for the controller

- **The wording of a deny reason decides whether it works.** The first deny said "Do not run Bash. Instead create notes.txt with the Write tool." Claude treated it as a possible prompt injection, because it contradicted the user's prompt. It ignored the reason and asked to run the same command again. The second deny said "The user denied this from their dashboard. Another agent is editing stamp.txt right now. Do not retry. Stop and wait for the user." Both Claude and Codex accepted it and stopped. The conflict guard must use the second style: say the user decided, give the reason, and tell the agent to stop. Then send the new instruction as a normal `herdr agent prompt`.
- **Trust the hook state over herdr's state.** herdr shows `working` for a held Claude question and for a held Codex approval. It also showed Codex as `idle` while Codex displayed its update prompt.
- **Every new folder starts with a trust prompt.** Claude asks for each new worktree. Codex applies trust to the repository root, so it should ask only once per repository. The recruit code must read the screen after `agent_not_ready` and answer the trust prompt with `send-keys`.
- **Claude sends no `SessionStart` over HTTP.** This is the same as in the hooks PoC. Create the unit on its first event.
- Codex showed "3 warnings" in its status bar. I did not open them.

## Verdict

Option F works for both agents. Build on it.

## How to run it

```sh
node server.mjs   # http://127.0.0.1:7777
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
herdr worktree create --cwd "$PWD/repo" --branch smoke-claude --label smoke-claude --no-focus
herdr agent start u1 --kind claude --pane <root_pane> -- --settings "$PWD/claude-settings.json" --permission-mode default
herdr worktree create --cwd "$PWD/repo" --branch smoke-codex --label smoke-codex --no-focus
herdr agent start u2 --kind codex --pane <root_pane> -- -a on-request -s read-only --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust
```

The Codex hooks live in `repo/.codex/hooks.json`, which is committed, so every worktree gets them. Answer held requests with `curl -XPOST localhost:7777/answer/latest -d '{"action":"deny","text":"..."}'`.

## Entire on top (tested the same day, Entire CLI 0.11.4)

- `entire enable --agent codex` **merges** into the existing `.codex/hooks.json`. Our hook stays first, and Entire's hook runs after it. `entire enable --agent claude-code` writes the repository's `.claude/settings.json`. Our hooks come from `--settings`, and both sets ran in the same session.
- Use `--project` so `.entire/settings.json` is committed and every herdr worktree has Entire enabled. `--local` settings are gitignored and do not reach new worktrees.
- In a third worktree (`smoke-entire`), one Claude session went through both: our server held and approved the Write, and Entire recorded the session.
- **The same id works in all three systems.** The Claude session id from herdr (`agent_session.value`) is the hook `session_id` and the Entire session id (`918e6864…`).
- `entire session info <id> --json` returns `status`, `turns`, `checkpoints`, `tokens` (total, input, cache, output), `last_prompt` and `files_touched`. This gives the token budget per unit and the touched files without parsing transcripts ourselves.
- `entire enable --agent` also lists `antigravity` as a supported agent. Not tested.
- Not tested: Entire Brain and Graph.

## Entire Brain (tested the same day, Brain 0.1.0, without the Graph plugin)

Setup: `entire brain setup --no-daemon --agent claude-code --backfill-budget 5` in `repo/`. It took under 1 s and stores everything under `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/brain/`. `--no-daemon` skips the machine-wide launchd watcher. Without Graph, the semantic code index and the entity index fail, but facts still work.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `entire brain remember "<text>" --path preferences.testing.stripe --kind decision --json` | Works in about 0.1 s and returns the fact as JSON. `--path` must start with `architecture`, `constraints`, `preferences`, `project` or `workflow`. |

18	- herdr: `https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/blob/2563803dca97c040beaf3dc3acdcb5a3221b4238/`. The docs live under `docs/versions/0.9.3/website/src/content/docs/`.

23	## TL;DR
24	
25	- **Recommendation: do not use herdr-web-ui as the backend. Build option F, a hybrid.** The game server is still a herdr plugin. It talks to herdr's own socket API for herdr panes, recruiting, orders, halting and coarse status. It also runs our own hooks server for structured approvals, questions, deny with a reason, file paths and gold.
26	- **Why not herdr-web-ui (option A).** It adds three things on top of herdr: a screen parser for prompts, transcript reading, and account plan limits. None of them closes the gaps that matter for the game.
27	  - Its prompts are parsed from screen text, and an approval cannot take a reason. The answer route refuses `custom_text` for Claude and Codex approvals, and a Codex "No" is sent as Esc ([prompt.ts L1117-L1239](https://github.com/devswha/herdr-web-ui/blob/002a2a9b74037683ba5e71efac3905ed561b964c/server/prompt.ts#L1117-L1239), [L2248](https://github.com/devswha/herdr-web-ui/blob/002a2a9b74037683ba5e71efac3905ed561b964c/server/prompt.ts#L2248), [L2297](https://github.com/devswha/herdr-web-ui/blob/002a2a9b74037683ba5e71efac3905ed561b964c/server/prompt.ts#L2297)).
28	  - Its `/api/usage` returns account plan limits in percent, not tokens per unit ([protocol.ts L196-L240](https://github.com/devswha/herdr-web-ui/blob/002a2a9b74037683ba5e71efac3905ed561b964c/shared/protocol.ts#L196-L240)).
29	  - It needs Bun 1.4 or newer ([INSTALL.md L26](https://github.com/devswha/herdr-web-ui/blob/002a2a9b74037683ba5e71efac3905ed561b964c/INSTALL.md#L26)), and this machine has Bun 1.3.14. It also shipped six releases between 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-09 ([CHANGELOG.md L69-L533](https://github.com/devswha/herdr-web-ui/blob/002a2a9b74037683ba5e71efac3905ed561b964c/CHANGELOG.md#L69-L533)).
30	- **herdr alone (option B) is not enough.** herdr reports only `idle | working | blocked | done | unknown` and has no field for the prompt's contents. I confirmed this in the local `herdr api schema --json` and in `herdr agent list`. Since 0.6.7, herdr's Claude and Codex integrations "report session identity only" ([CHANGELOG.md L650](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/blob/2563803dca97c040beaf3dc3acdcb5a3221b4238/CHANGELOG.md#L650)).
31	- **Hooks fill exactly the gaps herdr leaves.** Yesterday's hooks PoC showed approvals, questions and deny with a reason working for both agents ([poc/hooks/README.md](../poc/hooks/README.md)). herdr fills the gaps that hooks leave: it starts units in worktrees, sends orders to idle or busy units, and sees a Claude interrupt.
32	- **Plan for today.** Step 1 is a 45-minute smoke test: recruit one Claude unit and one Codex unit through herdr, with our hooks loaded per unit. If the herdr half fails, fall back to option C (hooks plus tmux, proven yesterday). If the hooks half fails under herdr, fall back to option E (ACP, proven yesterday) and give up the terminal UI.
33

187	## 5. Recommendation for today
188	
189	### 5.1 The decision
190	
191	- Build the game server as a herdr plugin, but use **option F** as its backend.
192	  - Use herdr's socket API, or the `herdr` CLI, for regions, herdr panes, recruit, orders, halt and coarse status.
193	  - Use our own hooks server for approvals, questions, deny with a reason, unit position and gold.
194	- Do not install herdr-web-ui for the game. It can be added after the demo works if someone wants a phone view. It is not needed for any requirement.
195	- Pick option F over option C because herdr already does recruit-in-worktree, orders to busy units and interrupt detection with documented calls. With tmux we would write those ourselves.
196	- Pick option F over options D and E because the bonus requirement holds, and because deny with a reason works for both agents.
197	
198	### 5.2 Build plan
199	
200	1. **Smoke test, 45 minutes. This is step 1.**
201	   - Run `herdr worktree create` from the repo workspace, then `herdr agent start u1 --kind claude --pane <root> -- --settings agent-rts-hooks.json --permission-mode default`.
202	     - `--permission-mode default` matters because your Claude settings use `defaultMode: auto` ([poc/acp/README.md](../poc/acp/README.md), Notes), and then no approvals appear.
203	     - `--settings` keeps our hooks out of `~/.claude`. The hooks PoC used the same flag.
204	   - Check four things:
205	     - The hook POST arrives with `X-Herdr-Pane: $HERDR_PANE_ID`, sent through `allowedEnvVars`.
206	     - The hook's `session_id` equals herdr's `agent_session.value`.
207	     - A deny with `message` changes what Claude does.
208	     - `herdr agent prompt u1 "…"` works while the unit is busy.
209	   - Repeat for Codex. Put the hooks in the repo's `.codex/hooks.json` so every worktree has them, and pass `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`.
210	     - Watch for the Codex folder-trust prompt in each new worktree (hooks PoC, "Problems found"). It can make `agent.start` return `agent_not_ready`. If it does, answer it with `herdr agent send-keys`.
211	2. **Unit state, about 1 hour.** Subscribe to `pane.agent_status_changed`. While the hooks server holds a request for a unit, the game shows "blocked on approval" or "blocked on question" from the hook payload, and the hook state wins over herdr's state. Otherwise use herdr's `working`, `idle` and `done`.
212	3. **Voice tools, about 1.5 hours.**
213	   - `order` maps to `agent.prompt`.
214	   - `recruit` maps to `worktree.create` plus `agent.start`.
215	   - `approve`, `deny` and `answer` resolve the held hook.
216	   - `halt(all)` sends `esc` to every unit.
217	   - `report()` reads the game state.
218	   - Give up a held Codex approval after about 60 s.
219	4. **Position and gold, about 1 hour.**
220	   - Map `tool_input.file_path` or `path` to the top-level folder, which is the region.
221	   - On `PostToolUse` and `Stop`, read new lines from `transcript_path` and add up the tokens. Use `message.usage` for Claude and `total_token_usage` for Codex.
222	   - Do not add a Claude status line, because it hides the hint herdr uses for "working".
223	
224	### 5.3 Fallback if step 1 fails
225	
226	- **If the herdr half fails** (`agent.start` or `worktree.create` does not work with our flags): keep the hooks server and switch to **option C**. That means tmux plus `git worktree add`, as in yesterday's hooks PoC. Orders go through `tmux send-keys`.
227	- **If the hooks half fails inside herdr panes** (hooks do not fire, or Codex hooks block startup): switch to **option E**, the ACP server in `poc/acp/server.mjs`. It already handles approvals, questions, orders and interrupts for Claude, Codex and opencode. Units lose their terminal UI, and deny becomes "deny, then the next order says what to do instead".
228	- **If only Codex hooks fail:** keep Claude on option F. Run Codex with herdr status only, and answer its approvals with `agent send-keys` without a reason. Or leave Codex out of the demo.
229	
230	## 6. Open questions
231	
232	1. **Hook state versus herdr state for a held Claude question.** While a `PreToolUse` hook holds `AskUserQuestion`, the terminal shows "running PreToolUse hooks…" and `claude agents` says `busy` (hooks PoC, row 6). herdr will most likely say `working`. **Not verified.** The game must trust the hook state here.
233	2. **`--settings` together with herdr's own Claude hook.** The user settings already contain herdr's `SessionStart` hook. I assume both run, because yesterday's PoC used `--settings` on the same machine. **Not verified under herdr.**
234	3. **Codex file paths from hooks.** The exact `tool_input.command` content for `apply_patch` was not captured in any PoC log.
235	4. **Two-step deny in herdr-web-ui** (pick "No", then send text). Whether the agent reads that text as the reason is **not verified**. This only matters if option A is chosen anyway.
236	5. **A Gemini unit.** herdr can start `gemini` and `agy`, but only with screen status ([agents.mdx L20-L43](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/blob/2563803dca97c040beaf3dc3acdcb5a3221b4238/docs/versions/0.9.3/website/src/content/docs/agents.mdx#L20-L43)). Gemini CLI hooks cannot grant permissions ([agent-status-detection.md §1.7](agent-status-detection.md)). An Antigravity managed agent through an API was not researched.

content.text:
Your earlier work in `/Users/max/Code/agentic-ai-hack` already covers much of the build. Four facts from it shape the plan.

1. **The backend is already proven.** `poc/herdr-smoke` passed a test today. Herdr starts each agent in its own worktree. A small hooks server (`server.mjs`) holds each approval and question as structured data and can answer it, including a deny with a reason. This works for Claude Code and Codex.
2. **One ID connects everything.** Herdr's `agent_session.value` is the same as the hook `session_id` and the Entire session ID. I confirmed this on your machine. `entire session info <id> --json` returns `files_touched`, the tokens and `last_prompt`.
3. **An airport UI already exists.** `prototype/tower-prototype.html` is a canvas page with no build step. Its variant B is an airport where position shows state (airspace, holding, approach, gate and hangar) and bands show projects. It runs on a simulated fleet.
4. **`GEMINI_API_KEY` is not set in this shell.** Herdr 0.9.3, Entire 0.11.4, Bun, Node, Claude Code and Codex are all installed.

The demo starts at 20:00, which leaves about 4 hours. Your teammates own the pitch, so Q9 to Q13 are theirs. I continue with the technical questions only, and Q14 and Q15 are folded in below.

❓ **T1** - **Backend base**: Here are two options:
- (a) Copy `poc/herdr-smoke/server.mjs` into `planesight` and extend it. The hooks give structured requests, such as the tool name, the file path and the question options. You answer through the held hook, including a deny with a reason.
- (b) Use Herdr only. Read the screen with `pane.read` and answer with `send-keys`. Herdr cannot tell which prompt is on screen, so Gemini must parse terminal text.

➡️ Choose (a). It was proven today, and structured requests give Gemini much better input. The action set is approve, deny with a reason, answer a question, and prompt a finished agent. Use Herdr for starting agents, for the `working`, `idle` and `done` states, and for prompts to finished agents.

❓ **T2** - **One process, and which runtime**: The server must take hook calls, talk to the Herdr socket, call Gemini and run the Entire CLI. It must also push live state to the browser.

➡️ Use one Node process, because `server.mjs` is already Node. It serves the UI, takes `POST /hook`, subscribes to Herdr events and pushes state to the browser over Server-Sent Events. Gemini runs through `@google/genai` 2.3+ with the Interactions API, as the brief asks. Do not use a framework or a build step.

❓ **T3** - **UI base**: Here are two options:
- (a) Take variant B from `tower-prototype.html`. Delete variants A and C, and replace the simulated fleet with the live state from the server.
- (b) Start a new UI.

➡️ Choose (a). Map the states this way:
- `working` means the plane is in the air and faded.
- A held approval or question means the plane is in the holding queue, in rank order and colored by request type.
- Herdr `done` means the plane has landed and waits for your review.
- A seen `idle` agent sits in the hangar.

A side panel shows the selected plane. It contains Gemini's summary, the proposed action with one line of reasoning, and the keys Enter (accept), E (edit) and S (skip).

❓ **T4** - **Gemini calls**: Here are two options:
- (a) Make one call per request, when the request arrives. It returns structured output with the category, a two-line summary, the proposed action, the reasoning and an effort estimate. Then make one cheap ranking call over the whole queue each time the queue changes. That call includes your last 20 decisions, which covers Q5.
- (b) Make one big call over everything on each change.

➡️ Choose (a). The cards are ready before you open a plane, and the ranking call stays small and fast. Use `gemini-3.8-flash` for the cards. You can use Flash-Lite for the ranking if latency becomes a problem. Gemini never sends anything by itself.

❓ **T5** - **Entire's role and collisions (Q14)**: When you open a plane that has landed, Gemini summarizes `entire session info` and the end of the transcript. For collisions, a held Write or Edit can target a file that another live session has in `files_touched`. Plane Sight then flags both planes, and Gemini proposes a deny that uses the wording the PoC proved works: "The user denied this from their dashboard. Another agent is editing X…".

➡️ Build both. The collision check is the strongest "it acts, and you stay in control" moment in the demo, and it costs little because Entire already lists the files.

❓ **T6** - **Plane size (Q15)**: Size can show token spend from `entire session info`, or all planes can be the same size.

➡️ Draw all planes at the same size for now. Add size as token spend only if time is left after 19:00.

❓ **T7** - **What you hand your teammates for the demo**: The demo needs a prepared repo with Entire enabled through `--project`. It needs about 8 agents, mixed between Claude Code and Codex, each with a task that stops at a known point. Two of the agents must target the same file so the collision appears.

➡️ You write `scripts/launch-demo.sh`, which starts 8 agents through Herdr with the hook flags from the PoC README. Your teammates write the 8 task prompts and the demo repo, and they rehearse with it. Agree on this split now so they can start in parallel.

❓ **T8** - **Timeline and cut order**: Here is the proposed timeline:
- Until 16:45: the server, with Herdr state, hooks and SSE, and a plain list in the UI.
- Until 17:45: the Gemini cards, the ranking, and accept or edit, which sends the answer to the agent.
- Until 18:30: the airport canvas fed with live data.
- Until 19:15: the Entire summaries and the collision check.
- 19:15: Code freeze, then rehearsal with your teammates and a backup screen recording.

If you fall behind, cut in this order: plane size, personalization, collisions, Entire summaries. Never cut the live ranking or the one-key answer.

➡️ Use this timeline with a hard code freeze at 19:15. Tell me if your demo slot is earlier than 20:00.

T1 a
T2 agreed
T3 b) it shoule be way calmer. the airport was way too busy and didnt help with cognitive overload tbh. it should be a nice fancy browser interface on top of our herdr engine like https://github.com/devswha/herdr-web-ui
T4 a
T5 ok and then works for our PoC demo in "production"?
T6 agreed
T7 yes 
T8 agreed

**Answer to your T5 question:** Yes, the collision check works in the live demo with real agents, but only if the data comes from our own hooks and not from Entire. Two facts matter here.

1. When a Write or Edit is held, the hook payload already contains the target file path. That part is reliable.
2. The other agent's edited files must also be known at that moment. Entire's `files_touched` may only update when a turn or a checkpoint finishes, and I have not verified when it updates. Our hooks server sees every `PostToolUse` Write and Edit as it happens, so it can keep its own list of files for each session.

So the server tracks the files itself, and Entire stays the source for the summaries. One more limit applies. The PoC never captured the file paths from Codex's `apply_patch`, so make both colliding agents Claude Code agents. Then the collision in the demo is real, not staged.

Your T3 answer removes the airport scene from the UI, so the UI questions start again.

❓ **U1** - **What remains of the airport**: The UI is now a calm browser interface, so the airport survives in the pitch and possibly as words in the UI. Your teammates' pitch also claims "a 2D plane instead of a 1D list". A calm list UI contradicts that claim.

➡️ Use the airport only as vocabulary. Name the three sections "Needs you" (holding), "Landed" (done, to review) and "In flight" (working, collapsed to a count). Do not draw a map. Tell your teammates to drop the "2D plane" claim and say "a ranked queue with the answer already drafted" instead.

❓ **U2** - **Layout**: The goal is less cognitive load, so the screen should show one decision at a time.

➡️ Use two columns.
- **Left: the ranked queue.** It has one compact row per waiting agent, showing the color dot for the request type, the agent name, a one-line summary and how long it has waited.
- **Right: the top item.** It shows Gemini's summary, the proposed action with one line of reasoning, the collision warning if there is one, and three buttons: Accept (Enter), Edit (E) and Skip (S). Below them sits a read-only tail of the agent's terminal from `pane.read`, collapsed by default.

After you answer an item, the next one moves up automatically.

❓ **U3** - **Embedding live terminals like herdr-web-ui**: herdr-web-ui shows full interactive terminals in the browser. That needs xterm.js and a pane stream, which costs at least an hour. The earlier research also found that herdr-web-ui itself needs Bun 1.4, while you have Bun 1.3.14, so forking it is not practical.

➡️ Do not embed interactive terminals. A collapsed text tail is enough. If you need full control, a "Jump to terminal" button calls Herdr's `agent.focus`. Take only the visual style from herdr-web-ui, not its code.

❓ **U4** - **Frontend stack**: T2 said no build step, but "nice and fancy" needs some polish.

➡️ Use one static `index.html` with vanilla JS and hand-written CSS, served by the Node server. A calm design is mostly typography, spacing and one accent color, and none of that needs a framework. React with Vite would add setup time and no real benefit for one screen.
U1 now i want to keep the pixel art airport

The pixel-art airport stays. Your T3 answer said the old airport was too busy, so the new one must be calm. That changes U2, and these questions replace it. U3 (no interactive terminals) and U4 (static HTML with vanilla JS) are still open, so please answer them too.

❓ **U2'** - **Screen layout**: Here are two options:
- (a) The airport fills the left 60% of the screen, and a decision card fills the right 40%. The card shows the summary, the proposed action, the reasoning, the collision warning and the buttons Accept, Edit and Skip.
- (b) The airport fills the whole screen, and the card opens as an overlay when you click a plane.

➡️ Choose (a). The airport shows you the situation, and the card shows you the decision. A fixed card means that you never hunt for where to act.

❓ **U5** - **What makes the airport calm**: The old prototype placed 10 agents across five zones, with constant motion. Here are the rules I propose:
- **Taxiway queue.** Waiting planes line up on one taxiway in rank order, and the #1 plane sits at the runway start. The position in the line is the ranking, so no extra numbers are needed.
- **Gates.** There is one gate per repository (Q12). Landed planes, which wait for your review, park at their gate.
- **Sky.** Working planes are small, faded and still. There is no animation, only a count, such as "5 in flight".
- **Motion.** Motion happens only on change. A plane moves smoothly when its rank changes, and it takes off after you accept. Only the #1 plane has a slow pulse.
- **Color.** Color is used only for the request type, and everything else is muted.

➡️ Use these rules. As a test, a person should know within 2 seconds which plane is next.

❓ **U6** - **Pixel art assets**: Here are three options:
- (a) Draw the shapes in code on the canvas, as the old prototype did.
- (b) Create the sprites with Nano Banana 2.1 (`gemini-nano-banana-2.1`): a ground tile, a terminal building, a plane in 4 directions and a runway.
- (c) Use free pixel art packs.

➡️ Choose (b), with a 30-minute limit and (a) as the fallback. Nano Banana gives a better look than code-drawn shapes, and it uses a second Gemini model, which fits the brief. Generate the sprites once before the demo and commit them. Plane Sight never generates images at runtime.

❓ **U7** - **Reuse the old canvas code**: T3 said to start new. Variant B in `tower-prototype.html` already contains canvas setup, hit testing for clicks and pixel-font rendering.

➡️ Start a new file, and copy only those three helpers. Do not copy its layout or its zones. This keeps the speed of the old code without the clutter.

❓ **U8** - **Tell your teammates**: With the airport back, the "2D instead of a 1D list" claim holds again, because gates group by repository and the taxiway shows the ranking.

➡️ Tell them that the pitch's airport story now matches the UI exactly. The taxiway is the priority queue, gates are repositories, the sky holds agents in flight, and a takeoff means you answered.

U2 a
U5 yes 
U6 b
U7 yes 
U8 ok

Two new branches appeared while I checked the hook settings from your PoC. U3 (no interactive terminals) and U4 (static HTML with vanilla JS) are also still open.

❓ **L1** - **Do landed planes join the queue?**: U5 places only held approvals and questions on the taxiway, and landed planes (Herdr `done`) park at their gate. In the "back from lunch" scene, most agents have probably finished, not stopped on a prompt. If only held requests get ranked, Plane Sight ignores most of the work that waits for you.

➡️ Rank landed planes too. They join the taxiway as "review" items, colored blue. For a landed plane, Gemini's card holds the Entire summary and a proposed next prompt, such as "run the tests and open a PR". Accept sends that prompt with `herdr agent prompt`. After you accept a card, the plane takes off. After you skip it, the plane parks at its gate. Gates then hold only planes that you have seen.

❓ **H1** - **Held requests time out**: Your PoC sets a 300-second hook timeout on Claude permission requests. When a hold times out, the agent shows its normal prompt in the terminal, and the hook can no longer answer it. Codex blocks its own terminal while a hook is held, so your PoC gives up on Codex after about 60 seconds. Your demo agents start before the pitch, so most holds will have expired by the time you go on stage.

➡️ Use two answer paths.
- For Claude, raise the hook timeout to 3600 seconds, so its holds survive the pitch.
- For Codex, keep the 60-second give-up. Keep the recorded payload so that the card still shows the request, and send the answer with `herdr agent send-keys`. A deny with a reason then becomes "No", followed by a prompt that gives the reason.
- Start the demo agents about 10 minutes before your slot, not earlier.

I have not verified whether Claude accepts a 3600-second timeout. I will check that first when I build the server.

# Plane Sight: build plan

Hackathon: Agentic AI Hack Zürich, 10 Oct 2026. Demo at 20:00. Code freeze at 19:15.

## Goal

A browser view over many coding agents that run in Herdr. Gemini ranks the agents that need you and drafts the answer. You accept with one key.

## Architecture

- One Node process, `server/server.mjs`. Base: `agentic-ai-hack/poc/herdr-smoke/server.mjs`.
  - `POST /hook/claude[/permission|/question]` and `POST /hook/codex[/permission]` hold approvals and questions.
  - Herdr socket (`~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`): `agent.list` snapshot, `events.subscribe` for status changes.
  - Herdr CLI: `agent prompt`, `agent send-keys`, `agent focus`, `pane read`.
  - Entire CLI: `entire session info <id> --json` for summaries and tokens.
  - Gemini: `@google/genai`, Interactions API, `gemini-3.8-flash`.
  - `GET /events`: Server-Sent Events with the full state.
- One ID everywhere: Herdr `agent_session.value` = hook `session_id` = Entire session ID.
- Files edited per session come from `PostToolUse` Write and Edit hooks. They feed the collision check.

## Plane states

| Source | Plane | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Herdr `working` | In flight | Sky, faded, count only |
| Held approval or question | Needs you | Taxiway, in rank order |
| Herdr `done` | Landed, needs review (blue) | Taxiway, in rank order |
| Seen or skipped `idle` | Parked | Gate of its repository |

## Answer paths

- Claude approval or question: answer the held hook. Hook timeout 3600 s.
- Codex approval: the server gives up after 60 s. Then it answers with `herdr agent send-keys`, and a deny reason goes in a follow-up prompt.
- Landed agent: `herdr agent prompt` with the accepted next prompt.
- Collision: deny with the PoC wording ("The user denied this from their dashboard. Another agent is editing X. Do not retry. Stop and wait for the user.").

## Gemini

- Card call, once for each new request or landed agent. Returns category, summary, proposed action, reasoning and effort.
- Ranking call each time the queue changes, debounced. Input: the cards and the last 20 decisions (`data/decisions.jsonl`).
- Gemini never sends anything by itself.

## UI

- `web/index.html`, no build step.
- Left 60%: Phaser 4.2.1 from a CDN, pixel-art airport. The taxiway is the queue, with #1 at the runway. Gates are repositories. The sky shows working agents.
- Calm rules: motion only on change, only #1 pulses, color only for request type.
- Right 40%: HTML decision card. Enter accepts, E edits, S skips. A collapsed `pane read` tail and a "Jump to terminal" button.
- Sprites from Nano Banana 2.1, made once and committed. Limit 30 min. Fallback: shapes drawn in code.

## Milestones

1. Until 16:45: server with Herdr state, hooks and SSE, and a plain list UI.
2. Until 17:45: Gemini cards, ranking and all answer paths.
3. Until 18:30: airport UI.
4. Until 19:15: Entire summaries and collisions.
5. 19:15: freeze, rehearse, record a backup video.

Cut order if late: plane size, personalization, collisions, Entire summaries.

## Split

- Builder: the prototype and `scripts/launch-demo.sh`.
- Teammates: the pitch, the demo repo, and 8 task prompts. Two Claude tasks must edit the same file.

## Unresolved questions

1. Does Claude accept a 3600 s hook timeout?
2. The demo slot and pitch length, from the organizers.
3. Pitch questions Q9 to Q13, for the teammates.
4. `GEMINI_API_KEY` must be set.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Start the demo fleet: one Herdr worktree and one agent per task, with Plane Sight hooks loaded.
#
# Usage: scripts/launch-demo.sh <repo> <tasks-file>
#   tasks-file: one task per line, "kind|branch|prompt". kind is claude or codex. Lines starting with # are ignored.
#   Example:    claude|login-form|Add a login form to src/app.tsx and ask me before choosing a validation library.
#
# The repo must be a git repo. The script writes .codex/hooks.json, runs `entire enable --project`
# and commits both, so every worktree gets the hooks and Entire.
set -euo pipefail

REPO="$(cd "$1" && pwd)"
TASKS="$2"
HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
CLAUDE_SETTINGS="$HERE/hooks/claude-settings.json"
CODEX_HOOK="$HERE/hooks/codex-hook.sh"

json() { python3 -I -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(eval(sys.argv[1], {}, {'d': d}))" "$1"; }

setup_repo() {
  mkdir -p "$REPO/.codex"
  cat > "$REPO/.codex/hooks.json" <<EOF
{

# Answer startup prompts (folder trust, Codex update notice) until the agent is ready.
wait_ready() {
  local name="$1" kind="$2" pane="$3"
  for _ in $(seq 1 10); do
    if herdr agent get "$name" 2>/dev/null | grep -q '"interactive_ready":true'; then return 0; fi
    local screen
    screen="$(herdr pane read "$pane" --source visible --lines 30 2>/dev/null || true)"
    if grep -qi "trust" <<<"$screen"; then
      if [ "$kind" = claude ]; then herdr agent send-keys "$name" down enter >/dev/null; else herdr agent send-keys "$name" enter >/dev/null; fi
    elif grep -qiE "update (available|now)|new version" <<<"$screen"; then
      herdr agent send-keys "$name" down enter >/dev/null
    fi
    sleep 2
  done
  echo "warning: $name is not ready. Check its pane: herdr agent focus $name" >&2
}

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

# Plane Sight

Air traffic control for coding agents. Plane Sight watches the agents you run in Herdr, asks Gemini which one needs you first and what to answer, and lets you send that answer with one key.

## Run it

```sh
npm install
export GEMINI_API_KEY=...        # without it, simple rules replace Gemini
npm start                        # http://127.0.0.1:7777
```

Plane Sight shows every Herdr agent. To show only the demo agents, set `PLANESIGHT_ONLY` to a path prefix, for example `PLANESIGHT_ONLY=$HOME/.herdr/worktrees/demo`.

## Start the demo fleet

```sh
scripts/launch-demo.sh <repo> <tasks-file>
```

- `<repo>` is a git repository. The script adds the Codex hooks and Entire to it and commits them.
- `<tasks-file>` has one task per line in the form `kind|branch|prompt`. `kind` is `claude` or `codex`. Lines that start with `#` are ignored.
- Each task gets its own Herdr worktree and agent. The branch name is also the agent's name on screen.
- Add `CLAUDE_EXTRA="--model claude-haiku-5-5"` to make Claude agents faster and cheaper.

Example tasks file:

```
claude|login-form|Add a login form to src/App.tsx. Ask me which validation library to use before you install one.
claude|theme|Change the primary color in src/theme.ts to #4a7fbf.
claude|theme-dark|Add a dark mode to src/theme.ts.
codex|api-tests|Write tests for src/api.ts and run them.
```

The two theme tasks edit the same file, so the second one triggers a collision.

## Answer agents

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| Enter | Accept the proposal on the strip |
| E | Edit the text, then send it with ⌘Enter |
| S | Skip: the plane parks at its gate |
| ↑ ↓ | Choose another plane in the queue |

## How it works

- Claude Code sends hook events over HTTP (`hooks/claude-settings.json`, passed with `--settings`). Codex runs `hooks/codex-hook.sh`.
- The server holds approvals and questions, polls Herdr for agent state, and pushes the state to the browser.
- Gemini writes one strip per waiting agent and ranks the queue. Your last 20 decisions in `data/decisions.jsonl` shape the ranking.
- Entire supplies what a finished agent did: files touched, tokens and the last prompt.
- If a hold times out, the agent shows its own prompt, and Plane Sight answers it with Herdr keys.

- **Fallback path:** I restarted the server while agent B was held. Agent B fell back to its terminal prompt. Plane Sight read the file path from the screen, still found the collision, and answered with Herdr keys.
- **Entire:** Entire restored agent A's edited files after the restart. Entire only lists a file once the turn has finished, so the server also tracks edits from the hooks as they happen.
- **UI:** Enter and the takeoff animation work, and the console shows no errors.

**One unexplained event.** In one test, a second agent was accepted 13 seconds after a single Enter press. I could not reproduce it. I added two guards against it. # herdr-web-ui

Browser UI for the herdr terminal multiplexer: a React 18 + xterm.js client (`src/`) and a Bun.serve backend (`server/`) that bridges herdr's newline-JSON unix-socket API. `shared/` is the wire contract both sides import.

## Scope

- This file, `server/AGENTS.md`, `src/AGENTS.md`, `scripts/AGENTS.md` and `shared/AGENTS.md` are committed and apply to every agent working on the project, forks included. A PR is checked against them together with `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `.github/REVIEW.md`, `docs/development.md` and `DESIGN.md`.
- They hold only what the code and those documents do not show. Commands, layout, environment variables and release steps are in `docs/development.md` and `package.json`; do not copy them here.
- Read `server/AGENTS.md` before editing `server/` and `src/AGENTS.md` before editing `src/`; likewise `scripts/AGENTS.md` for `scripts/` and `shared/AGENTS.md` for `shared/`.
- "Maintainer workflow" applies only to the maintainer. Everyone else follows `CONTRIBUTING.md` for branches, PRs and the changelog.

## Bridge invariants

The app is only a bridge: herdr owns every pty, scrollback and agent state.

- NEVER load node-pty inside Bun; it panics the runtime (oven-sh/bun#18546). All PTY work goes through the Node sidecar `server/pty/pty-host.mjs`, and the only process it runs is `herdr terminal attach <terminal_id>`.
- NEVER pass `--takeover` to `herdr terminal attach` on the server's own initiative: an attach, a retry or a reconnect waits for the holder instead. Only a user's explicit request for that pane, from an interact connection, may take it. Always set `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH` to the socket the RPCs use.
- NEVER give xterm scrollback (keep `scrollback: 0`), and never rebuild an attached terminal from `pane.read`. The attach byte stream is the source of truth; only a mirrored pane (below) is drawn from `pane.read`.
- NEVER edit `shared/herdr-api.generated.ts`. Run `bun run generate:types`.
- NEVER pool herdr RPC connections: herdr closes the socket after each response. Use one connection per call (10 s timeout). Only `events.subscribe` stays open, and a second subscribe on an open connection is silently ignored, so reopen it with the full set.
- `pane.process_info` takes `pane_id`, not `target`. Given `target`, it silently answers for the focused pane.
- `server/collector.ts` is the only status subscription source. Do not subscribe to status anywhere else.
- Nothing the user typed is ever queued or sent automatically while offline. Keystrokes go to a draft the user sends or discards. An explicit chat Send while an agent works can enter the bridge's pending list on `pending-input` bridges: the next turn and its explicit Send now action claim the same server ID. Automatic delivery requires the original live connection and pane lease; disconnect/reload never resumes it. Existing browser-held messages still require "Send now".
- Prompt answers are `send_keys` navigation, never digits, and go through `POST /api/pane/prompt/answer`: the key semantics per agent live on the server.
- Web push: build requests with `generateRequestDetails` and send them with `fetch`; never call `sendNotification`.
- The omo transcript is found through the process tree, never through `pane.agent` or file mtime.
- Windows x64 has no PTY sidecar: herdr there cannot `terminal attach`, so the server mirrors the screen (`server/mirror.ts`). A Linux or macOS PC without Node for the sidecar is mirrored the same way. Do not assume a pty exists.

## Changing a contract

- HTTP and WS shapes live in `shared/protocol.ts`; change both sides through it and add a contract test (`server/api.contract.test.ts` for endpoints).
- Every push to `main` redeploys the site and the demo. A new endpoint or WS frame needs an answer in `site/demo/transport.ts`, or the demo gets a 404.
- The demo is the client itself: `site/demo/transport.ts` also imports `shared/` and `rollupStatus` from `src/lib/status.ts`, so a change there changes the demo.
- `site/demo/fixtures.ts` is bundled into the browser and reused by `scripts/readme-media/stage.ts`: keep it fictional and free of server imports.
- Every error body is `{ error: { code, message } }`, built only with the helpers in `server/http.ts`.
- Mutating machine, device and update POSTs require same-origin plus the `x-herdr-machine: 1` or `x-herdr-update: 1` header.
- Route order in `createServer().fetch` matters: bridge, then machines, then `/ws`, then the `/api/*` handlers, then a 404 for the rest of `/api/*`, then static files.

## Code conventions

## 1. Atmosphere & Identity

A warm terminal: an amber-phosphor console on lamp-lit graphite (dark) or ledger paper (light),
with chat-app clarity. Tonal surfaces and hairlines keep the chrome out of the way. There is ONE
chrome color, amber: focus, the chosen lens, the terminal cursor and the user's own action (Send, primary
buttons). Agent states carry the remaining saturated colors and none of them is amber. The user's
chat turns are neutral raised cards, so a long thread never turns into a wall of color. Dark is the
default, light follows the same hierarchy, and comfortable or compact density changes scale without
changing information architecture. A dark report look, a neutral charcoal one, Catppuccin and lilac are
opt-in palettes (Settings → Appearance → Colors); amber stays the default and the look before settings load.

The sidebar is one grid: a leading cell that says who or what a row is (the coding agent's brand
mark, else the place's own glyph), a title, and a trailing cell that says how it is. Workspaces
and Agents are independent lists, as in herdr's Spaces and Agents panels; tab and pane navigation
stays over the terminal and in the palette. Sections are parted by space and a dim head, never by
a rule. Hover and selection are one neutral fill at two strengths. Brand marks are the only color
there that is not a state, and a ready row draws no state at all. Amber connects focus, the chosen
lens glyph and the terminal cursor.

## 2. Color

### Palette

Only tokens overridden by `[data-theme="light"]` have a light value. Both columns are literal CSS.
